lead: Don't just keep cleaning up the consequences; look for what you could change so problems happen less.
when: When the same kind of problem keeps happening, the fixes keep getting busier, or you suspect people are being pushed along by certain rules or ways information is arranged.
body:
Your team chases the same kind of task every day. You send more reminders, which seems to help briefly, but a few days later things are back to how they were. Maybe the problem isn't too few reminders. Maybe it's unclear who owns the task, priorities that conflict, or nobody being able to see what the next step is waiting for.

A leverage point is a place to intervene in an interconnected system where a change can have a large effect on the system's overall behavior, such as its information flows, rules, feedback structures, or goals.

Leverage points remind us to shift our attention from a single consequence to the structure that produces it: who gets what information, how responsibility is assigned, what behavior the rules encourage, and what the whole system is actually pursuing. Adjusting these can change the course of things more than endless patching.

But "high impact" doesn't mean "easy to change." Some rules need many people to agree, and some adjustments have unexpected effects. Even after finding a cause that sounds fundamental, you still need to explain how the change would work, test it, and watch what happens.

The structure diagram connects the surface problem to information, rules, and feedback. Mark the relationship you plan to change, then draw the expected effects and possible side effects. These arrows are explanations to be tested, not a proven chain of cause and effect.
example:
Your team's shared documents are always out of date, and every week people ask, "Where's the latest version?" Reposting the file in the group chat over and over only solves the search problem for the moment.

Another approach is to set one fixed place to find things, name an owner and an update date for each document, and make old links point to the current version. These changes alter how information flows and who's responsible for keeping it up. Try it with one type of document first and see whether repeat questions, wrong versions, and upkeep effort go down before deciding whether to roll it out.
extra:
Meetings often run long, and the host keeps urging everyone to talk faster. Look deeper at the structure, and it might turn out that nobody said in advance which decision needs to be made or who should bring what materials, so time gets spent filling in background on the spot.

Try writing down the meeting's goal, the needed materials, and how the decision will be made ahead of time. It won't guarantee every meeting gets shorter, but it's more likely to uncover why meetings keep running over than blaming everything on how fast one person talks.
steps: Map out the people, information, rules, and feedback involved, and find how the problem keeps getting produced.
Propose one structural change that could shift behavior, and spell out which relationship it works through to affect the outcome.
Start in a small area that's negotiable and observable, check the overall effect and side effects, then decide whether to keep it or change it.
caution: This isn't a promise that one button will fix everything. Systems have delays, interactions, and outside changes, and a local improvement can shift the burden onto someone else. The theory of constraints focuses on the bottleneck limiting the system's current overall output, while leverage points look more broadly at where to intervene to change how a system behaves.
exercise: Pick a small problem that keeps coming back and write down two things: "What I keep patching up" and "What arrangement keeps bringing it back." Then propose one rule or information change you could test on a small scale.
brief: A stick figure adjusts a small rule gear in a system, rerouting task blocks that kept getting stuck; faintly beside it, someone pushes a single block without changing the structure.
diagramCaption: Information, tasks, and rules together shape the outcome. The tool at the top points to a rule that can be adjusted, and the dashed return line is a reminder to watch for later changes rather than judging by one local improvement.
sources: Donella Meadows · Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System
